answer_text:
We need the smallest possible size of a color set \(A\) for a coloring \(f:\mathbb N^*\to A\) such that numbers whose difference is prime receive different colors.

### 1. Lower bound: at least \(4\) elements are necessary

Consider the four positive integers

\[
1,\;3,\;6,\;8.
\]

Their pairwise absolute differences are

\[
\begin{aligned}
|3-1|&=2,\\
|6-1|&=5,\\
|8-1|&=7,\\
|6-3|&=3,\\
|8-3|&=5,\\
|8-6|&=2.
\end{aligned}
\]

All of these are prime numbers. Therefore, by the required property, the four values

\[
f(1),\; f(3),\; f(6),\; f(8)
\]

must all be distinct. Hence

\[
|A|\ge 4.
\]

### 2. Upper bound: \(4\) elements are sufficient

Take

\[
A=\{0,1,2,3\}
\]

and define

\[
f(n)\equiv n \pmod 4.
\]

Suppose \(|i-j|\) is a prime number \(p\). Since \(p\) is prime, \(p\) is not divisible by \(4\). Indeed, the only even prime is \(2\), and all other primes are odd. Thus

\[
p\not\equiv 0 \pmod 4.
\]

Therefore,

\[
i\not\equiv j \pmod 4,
\]

so

\[
f(i)\neq f(j).
\]

Thus a coloring with \(4\) colors exists.

Combining the lower and upper bounds, the minimum number of elements that \(A\) must have is

\[
\boxed{4}
\]
